lessons.title: Kingdoms and empires of pre-colonial Africa
lessons.programRef: GCE O Level History — African societies before European rule (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name major African states before colonial rule
Describe the trans-Saharan trade and its effects
Describe typical features of political, economic and social organisation
reviewNotes: Historian to verify approximate periods: Ghana c. 700–1100 (some say from earlier centuries), Mali c. 1200–1450, Songhai c. 1460–1591; the Moroccan invasion of Songhai (1591); the examples of states; and the description of goods exchanged. Dates shown as approximate.

Draft for historian review: only widely accepted facts and approximate dates are used; every date, name and interpretation must be verified by a history teacher before release. Political questions are stated neutrally.

blocks.md: Long before Europeans ruled Africa, many states, kingdoms and empires existed. In West Africa the great savanna empires of **Ghana**, **Mali** and **Songhai** grew rich from trade in gold, salt and other goods. Others include **Kanem-Bornu** near Lake Chad, the Yoruba kingdom of **Oyo**, **Benin**, and the **Asante** kingdom. In other parts of Africa there were other states and also societies without kings, governed by councils of elders.

blocks.caption: Three West African empires (approximate periods)
blocks.alt: A timeline with three overlapping bars for Ghana, Mali and Songhai between 700 and 1600.

blocks.title: Trans-Saharan trade
blocks.md: Caravans of camels crossed the Sahara between North Africa and West Africa for centuries. Gold, kola, ivory and slaves went north; salt, cloth, horses and manufactured goods went south. Towns such as Timbuktu and Gao became centres of trade and learning. The trade also spread Islam, writing and new ideas across the Sahel.

**Government.** Many states had a king or chief with advisers and councils, an army, tax or tribute, and officials. Some societies were organised by clans and age groups. **Economy.** Most people farmed, herded or fished; craftsmen worked iron, wood, leather and cloth; local markets and long-distance trade connected regions. **Society.** Family, lineage and religion were central, and culture was passed on through oral tradition, music and craft.

blocks.title: Be careful with dates
blocks.md: Dates for early African states are **approximate** and historians disagree about them. Give 'about' or 'c.' and the century, not exact years, unless you are sure. Do not say that Africa had no history before colonial rule or treat 'tribe' as a primitive label; there were complex states and trade networks.

blocks.title: Effects of the trade and the states
blocks.md: Strong states protected trade routes and encouraged crafts and learning. Wealth and ideas moved between regions. Trade also led to wars and the capture of people. The empires declined for many reasons, including internal quarrels and outside attack.

blocks.title: Example 1: describe the trade
blocks.statement: Explain why salt and gold were exchanged in the trans-Saharan trade.
steps: Salt was scarce in the savanna but available in the Sahara.
Gold came from the south and was valued in North Africa.
Each region wanted what it lacked, so both sides gained.
blocks.answer: Each side exchanged what the other lacked.

blocks.title: Example 2: sequence the empires
blocks.statement: Put in order of rise: Songhai, Ghana, Mali.
steps: Ghana is the earliest of the three savanna empires.

lessons.programRef: GCE O Level History — African societies before European rule (to be checked)

objectives: Name major groups and political systems in what is now Cameroon
Describe the fondoms, lamidats and coastal trading societies
Explain how geography shaped the way people lived
reviewNotes: Historian to verify: the Bamum script (invented under King Njoya, c. 1896 onwards), the Fulani lamidats of the 19th century, Bafut and Grassfields details, goods traded, and the general description of settlement; confirm which peoples the syllabus expects to be named.

Draft for historian review: only widely accepted facts and approximate dates are used; every date, name and interpretation must be verified by a history teacher before release. Political questions are stated neutrally.

blocks.md: Cameroon has always been a meeting place of peoples. Bantu-speaking, Semi-Bantu, Sudanic and other groups settled over many centuries. By the 1800s the land contained many different political systems: powerful **chiefdoms (fondoms)** in the Grassfields, kingdoms such as the **Bamum**, **lamidats** in the north, coastal trading communities, and many smaller communities led by councils of elders.

Coast: Duala and other Sawa trading peoples

blocks.caption: Some peoples of pre-colonial Cameroon (schematic sketch)
blocks.alt: Four boxes showing the north, west, centre-south and coast with names of peoples.

blocks.title: Examples of societies
blocks.md:
- **Grassfields chiefdoms** (West and North West), ruled by a **Fon** or chief with secret societies and councils; Bafut is a well-known example.
- **Bamum kingdom** around Foumban, known for its royal palace and later for a script created under King Njoya.
- **Northern Cameroon:** the **Fulani** established lamidats in the 1800s under Islamic leadership, alongside older groups such as the Mandara and Kotoko.
- **The coast:** the **Duala** and related peoples traded with European merchants.

**Geography** shaped life. Fertile volcanic highlands supported dense farming populations; the forest supported farmers, hunters and craftsmen; the savanna favoured herding and cotton growing. Markets and trade routes connected the forest, the highlands, the savanna and the coast, with iron tools, salt, cloth and food crops exchanged.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Many groups cannot be reduced to one description; this lesson is an outline.
- Do not present the chiefdoms as 'primitive': they had laws, armies, craftsmen and long-distance trade.
- Exact dates of founding and of reigns are often uncertain and must be given with care.

blocks.title: Contact with the coast
blocks.md: From the 1400s the coastal peoples met Portuguese and later other European traders. They exchanged goods such as cloth, metal, guns, alcohol and mirrors for local products such as palm oil, ivory and, in earlier centuries, slaves. Coastal chiefs controlled much of this trade and became wealthy and influential.

blocks.title: Example 1: link to geography
blocks.statement: Explain why the Grassfields supported many small chiefdoms with dense populations.
steps: The volcanic soils and cool climate were good for farming.
Good farmland supported many people living close together.
Hills and valleys encouraged separate communities, each with its own chief.
blocks.answer: Fertile soils and relief encouraged dense settlement and separate chiefdoms.

blocks.title: Example 2: coastal middlemen
blocks.statement: Why were coastal peoples such as the Duala powerful in trade with Europeans?
steps: The coast was where ships arrived.
Local chiefs controlled access to goods from the interior.
They acted as middlemen, buying from inland peoples and selling to ships.
blocks.answer: They controlled the trade as middlemen between inland peoples and European ships.
